title: Resetting for Growth, Jobs, and Economic Transformation (The Budget Statement and Economic Policy of the Government of Ghana for the 2026 Financial Year)
presented_by: Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson (MP), Minister for Finance, on the authority of President John Dramani Mahama

source_notes.page_numbering: All 'page' values are PDF page numbers of 2026-Budget-Statement-and-Economic-Policy.pdf (printed page = PDF page - 16 for the main body, e.g. printed p.1 = PDF p.17).
source_notes.units: Money in GH¢ million unless a field/unit says otherwise. Appendix figures (given in GH¢) were divided by 1,000,000 and rounded to 0.1.
source_notes.prior_year_basis: 2025 comparisons use the '2025 Budget Revised' column (mid-year revised budget), 'Prog Q1-Q3' targets, 'Prov Q1-Q3' provisional outturn (end-September 2025) and 'Proj Q1-Q4' projected end-year outturn from Appendices 2A-2C. The original March-2025 budget figures are not tabulated in this document except the headline macro targets on PDF p.26.

headline_summary: The 2026 Budget, the Mahama administration's second, is themed 'Resetting for Growth, Jobs, and Economic Transformation' and pivots from 2025's stabilisation (inflation down from 23.8% in Dec 2024 to 8% in Oct 2025, public debt down to 45% of GDP, a primary surplus of 1.6% of GDP by September) towards growth and jobs. It targets real GDP growth of at least 4.8%, end-year inflation of 8% and a 1.5%-of-GDP primary surplus, with total expenditure of GH¢302.5bn against revenue and grants of GH¢268.1bn (overall deficit 2.2% of GDP on commitment basis, 4.0% on cash basis) and a total appropriation of GH¢357.1bn. Flagship measures include GH¢30bn for Big Push roads, VAT reform (abolishing the COVID-19 levy, cutting the effective VAT rate from 21.9% to 20%, raising the registration threshold to GH¢750,000), GH¢29.8bn of arrears clearance plus GH¢15.2bn for energy-sector shortfalls, and new programmes in agriculture (Farmer Service Centres, oil palm), education (ending double-track, 600 new basic schools), health (MahamaCares, new regional hospitals), rural electrification and military retooling.

debt.restructuring_notes: Debt fell GH¢96.5bn (726.7bn -> 630.2bn) mainly from cedi appreciation; external debt down GH¢97.6bn (23.4%). By end-2024, 93.5% of debt restructured (US$20.4bn domestic notes/bonds, US$13.1bn Eurobonds, US$5.2bn bilateral); remaining 6.5% mainly commercial debt under negotiation (p.118). MoU with Official Bilateral Creditors effective 13 Oct 2025; bilateral agreements signed with China, Finland, France, Germany, Spain and UK, others expected by Dec 2025; AIPs reached with several commercial lenders (p.48). All DDEP coupons honoured: GH¢20.3bn (GH¢16.8bn cash, GH¢3.6bn in kind) (p.48). October 2025 DSA moved Ghana from high to moderate risk of debt distress (p.33) - note MTDS text (p.119) still states goal of returning to moderate risk by 2028. 2026 plans: resume benchmark domestic bond issuance, buybacks/bond exchanges, operational Sinking Fund (cedi and dollar accounts), Primary Dealer reform. MTDS benchmarks: debt maturing within 1 year <=15±5% of total; ATM >=8 years; T-bills <=20±5% of domestic debt; USD debt <=70% of external debt (p.119).
debt.interest_saving_note: Lower domestic rates reduced domestic debt service cost by nearly GH¢8.8bn (p.33).

shortfalls_admitted.text: Total revenue and grants for Q1-Q3 2025 were 4.7% below target (GH¢154.9bn vs GH¢162.6bn), with shortfalls in all major categories except non-oil non-tax revenue.
Non-oil tax revenue 4.1% below target; PAYE, CIT, VAT, excise, Growth & Sustainability Levy and import duties underperformed.
Oil and gas receipts 52.2% below target (GH¢5.9bn vs GH¢12.4bn).
Grant disbursements only GH¢963m vs GH¢1.9bn target due to development-partner delays.
Capital expenditure 59.0% below target (GH¢10.9bn vs GH¢26.6bn); foreign-financed capex delayed by bilateral debt restructuring.
Compensation of employees exceeded target (GH¢58.1bn vs GH¢57.5bn); wages and salaries overshot by 2.0%.
Project loan disbursements GH¢2.8bn vs GH¢8.7bn target.
ABFA inflows US$139.3m short of target; only US$1.9m utilised and no Big Push disbursement from ABFA by end-September.
Petroleum receipts down 35.7% y/y; daily oil output fell from 200,000 bpd (2019) to ~150,000 bpd; annual output from 71.4m to ~36m barrels.
GH¢8.6bn of arrears claims remain under review for inadequate documentation.
Inflation annual average 18.7% at end-Sept 2025 - ECOWAS 5% criterion not achieved.
Two of eleven IMF structural benchmarks (June-Sept) not yet implemented.
COCOBOD still has 90,000mt (~US$234m) of low-priced forward contracts to regularise; cocoa roads made up 66.8% of COCOBOD debt.
Receiver needs ~GH¢2.0bn to pay 55,376 depositors of failed S&Ls; ~GH¢5.0bn of FMC investor funds at risk; FMC asset recovery GH¢965m vs GH¢1.4bn target.
Banking NPL ratio still 20.4%.
Energy-sector business-as-usual shortfall projected at US$1.6bn for 2025.
Credit growth subdued; private sector credit growth slowed to 13.3% from 15.1%.
Abuse of Import Declaration Forms: US$31bn transferred abroad with no imports; ~GH¢11bn revenue lost through under-declaration.
US$40m paid to ELBIT for 19 APCs under a 2020 contract with no APC delivered.
Navy faces ageing fleet and uncompleted Ezinlibo FOB; Air Force ageing fleet; Fire Service lacks basic equipment.
Double-track SHS system persists; 30 E-Blocks abandoned; Agenda 111 hospitals and La General, Effia Nkwanta, KATH maternity and Sewua hospitals described as abandoned.
La General Hospital only 33% complete.
Livestock vaccination at 44% of target; vaccine procurement 587,014 of 1.7m doses.
Tree for Life 17m of 30m seedlings; timber exports at 51% of annual target.
Audit Service completed 79.83% of its annual audit target.
Birth registration covered only 62.4% of expected births and 47% of deaths.
Big Push and other road corridors still incomplete (Accra-Kumasi dualisation 64%, Tema-Akosombo 58%).
Food glut across the country required an extra GH¢200m for buffer-stock purchases.
Procurement thresholds last reviewed in 2016 - District Assemblies can no longer build a six-unit classroom block within their threshold.
Ghana Petroleum Funds earned only US$194.9m on US$1.46bn reserves since 2011 (~1% a year).
DACF 2025 projected transfer GH¢5,102.4m against revised budget GH¢7,683.6m (appendix).
2024 imports of GH¢204bn (CIF) but only GH¢85bn taxable - misclassification and under-invoicing at ports.

Illegal mining threatening water bodies and forests (p.84)
Climate shocks - drought in northern Ghana and flooding in Greater Accra (p.73)
Delays in donor/project loan disbursements and low capital budget execution (pp.35, 38-39)

data_quality_notes: Text says the overall commitment deficit will 'narrow from 1.8% of GDP in 2025 to 2.2% in 2026' and the cash deficit will 'improve from 2.8% to 4.0%' - both actually widen (p.112).
Q1-Q3 2025 total expenditure: text GH¢175.9bn (12.6% GDP, p.37) vs Appendix 2A GH¢178,444.0m (12.7%, p.170).
Non-oil GDP 2025 projection: Table 13 (p.108) 5.3% vs Appendix 1C (p.167) 6.2%; 2026: 4.9% vs 5.0%.
Public debt end-Sept 2025 is 48.9% of GDP in ECOWAS Table 5 (p.25) vs 45.0% end-Oct in text/Appendix 10A.
Debt rule: 'below 45% by 2035' (p.32) vs '45% by 2034' (p.163). Cedi appreciation: 34.6% (p.57) vs 34.9% (p.162).
Medium-term table (Table 14, p.112) differs slightly from Appendix 3A for 2027-2028 balances (e.g. cash deficit 2027 -2.4 vs -2.5).
Domestic financing 2026: text GH¢71.0bn (p.116) vs Appendix 3A GH¢71,972.6m (p.175).
24-Hour Economy 2026: text GH¢110m (p.157) vs appendix line GH¢90m (p.196). Buffer Stock: GH¢200m (p.157) vs appendix GH¢105m (p.197). Garment factory jobs: ~27,000 (p.146) vs >20,000 (p.161).
Oil palm finance: US$500m window (p.137) vs 'GH¢6.9 billion' window (p.157).
Rural electrification Phase I: text names four regions (Volta, Oti, Savannah, Central, p.135); appendix line says 'Three (3) Regions' (p.197).
Textbook beneficiaries differ: KG books for ~1 million learners (p.148) vs ~200,000 (p.158); JHS3 books 1 million (p.148) vs 500,000 (p.158).
Appendix 2C (p.173) Big Push sub-lines for 2025 Q1-Q3 (GH¢10,225.4m) exceed total domestic capex outturn (GH¢7,217.7m) - internally inconsistent; not used.
Appendix 3B shows grants at 0.6% of GDP for 2026 though GH¢3,066m is ~0.2% (Figure 9, p.114).
Greater Accra MMDA ceilings page header reads '2025 MMDAs Indicative Ceilings' while other regions say 2026 (p.224).
MTDS (p.119) states goal to 'return Ghana to a moderate risk of debt distress' by 2028 although p.33 says the Oct 2025 DSA already rates Ghana moderate risk.
